title: What I Saw at the Consumer Electronics Show
text:

https://www.barrons.com/articles/what-i-saw-at-the-consumer-electronics-show-51547256993 What I Saw at the Consumer Electronics Show By Jan. 11, 2019 8:36 p.m. ET Order Reprints Illustration by Robert DiIeso Text size
The annual Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas is always a must-stop for anyone interested in where technology is heading. This past week’s version was no different, with big themes like artificial intelligence, the smart home, and robots dominating many of the sprawling booths at the Las Vegas Convention Center. Here’s a sampling of what we saw and experienced.
We’ve heard from executives recently that trust is the No. 1 issue for tech in 2019, and CES proves their point. Alphabet ’s (ticker: GOOGL) Google went big with a preview of Google Assistant Connect—a platform for device makers to work with Google’s popular voice assistant—in a massive booth three times the size of last year’s. Amazon.com (AMZN) introduced several home-security devices, including WiFi-enabled smart locks and an app to control garage doors. The idea: to make life more convenient and organized. But in digitizing nearly every home appliance, privacy advocates fear consumers’ personal information will be increasingly vulnerable to hacks or sharing with third parties without their consent. To hammer home that message, Apple (AAPL) bought a multistory billboard looming above the Google exhibit with the ominous message: “What happens on your iPhone stays on your iPhone.”
If Samsung Electronics (005930.Korea) taught us anything at CES, it’s that artificial intelligence is the glue that binds together its vast array of products, and that it never hurts to cooperate with a rival. Samsung’s AI connects its robots, digital car cockpit, and the smart refrigerator, oven, dishwasher, dryer, and big-screen TV on its huge stage at CES, via its Bixby voice assistant.
Besides seamlessly connecting a broad product line of products, Samsung boasts of an open platform that allows it to dive into fledgling markets such as the Internet of Things, smart homes, and 5G without missing a beat. “We believe in consumers and their experiences; it’s stupid to exclude them” with closed computing environments, Samsung Senior Vice President Yoon Lee said, an apparent allusion to Apple’s “walled garden” business model.
That doesn’t mean Samsung and Apple can’t work together. The pair announced that Samsung would offer iTunes for movies and TV shows on its smart TVs, and let AirPlay stream content from Apple devices to Samsung televisions. Samsung’s eagerness to partner “comes from the realization by everyone that walled gardens don’t maximize business opportunities,” said Patrick Moorhead, principal analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy.
Much of what appears at CES is realistically a few years away. AI. 5G. Virtual reality. All whiz-bang stuff—just not right now. But Delta Air Lines (DAL), which handles 15,000 flights a day, is in the midst of a significant biometrics rollout while exploring ways to improve the travel experience for an estimated 180 million people it flies annually. “At our core, we’re a technology company,” Delta Chief Information Officer Rahul Samant said. “And what we’re looking for is personal-facing technology.”
A program begun in early December uses biometrics to let passengers navigate gates and Delta Sky Club lounges without having to repeatedly produce IDs. Delta customers who register with the biometric system still have to go through the checkpoint, but they are escorted to the head of the line.
Brilliant, the Silicon Valley start-up that developed what it calls the world’s first light switch to control smart-home devices, has teamed up with nearly every major company with a voice assistant—except Apple—until now. Apple and Brilliant announced at CES that the Brilliant Home Control is now integrated with Apple’s HomeKit, allowing consumers to find and control any light connected to Brilliant’s touch screen tablet by speaking to Siri or its Home app on any Apple device. Brilliant already works with Google Assistant, has Alexa built in, and provides native control over other smart-home devices. “As smart technology becomes more fundamental to the home experience, it is increasingly impractical to clutter tables and countertops throughout the home with appliances,” said Brilliant CEO and co-founder Aaron Emigh.
Apple, which does not attend CES, needs some good news after a brutal end to 2018. Apple also needs to establish more of a foothold in the smart-home market, which is expected to grow 14% to $35.9 billion in 2019, according to Statista.com.
Now for the fun. Barron’s hopped into a driverless BMW 540 for a 5.5-mile spin that lasted 25 minutes. The company behind the technology, auto parts supplier Aptiv (APTV), has deployed 30 vehicles in Sin City via a Lyft app that has been used commercially some 30,000 times since May.
The ride was the most impressive since we started taking driverless demos five years ago. Improvements in so-called in-lane biasing, or ILB, allow vehicles to navigate more confidently, even when another car edges into the lane. The car can change lanes to move around others and maneuvered around people at intersections. Of course, they’re not perfect. They still have issues at intersections, where cars and people are simultaneous moving in multiple directions. And they can’t honk to warn of imminent problems.
